# Inflation Targeting in Latin America — Vittorio Corbo & Klaus Schmidt-Hebbel 2001

**Type:** paper
**Tags:** #inflation-targeting #latin-america #exchange-rate-regimes #sacrifice-ratio #inflation-expectations #credibility #chile
**Source:** Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile, Documento de Trabajo Nº 230 (Noviembre 2002; www.economia.puc.cl); this version Jan. 12, 2001, prepared for the Workshop in Open Economy Macroeconomics and International Finance, Catholic University of Chile, January 15-18, 2001
**Language:** English
**Source file:** [[external/clean_md/it_latin_america (Corbo & Schmidt-Hebbel, 2001)]]

---

## Context and motivation

Latin America had the world's highest inflation until the early 1990s, the product of decades of fiscal dominance; in the 1980s regional inflation averaged 145% a year. Around 1990 most countries launched stabilizations, and by the end of the decade regional inflation was below 10%. At the same time the region was abandoning intermediate exchange rate regimes after a decade of misalignments and crises, moving to dollarization or currency boards at one end and to free floats at the other. A float needs a nominal anchor other than the exchange rate, and inflation targeting (IT) was becoming that anchor in Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Peru. The paper asks how the regime choice is made, how the Latin American targeters compare with targeters and non-targeters elsewhere, how they implement IT, and — for Chile, the longest experience — whether announcing a target changed inflation expectations and so the cost of disinflation. The authors are a Catholic University professor and the Central Bank of Chile's chief of research.

## Core argument / thesis

Under exchange rate flexibility the best available anchor is the announced inflation target, because it neither depends on a stable money demand (which high inflation destroys) nor exposes the economy to the credibility and financial-fragility problems of a peg. The target works mainly through **inflation expectations**: as it gains credibility it pulls expectations down, which lowers wage and price inflation directly and changes their dynamics. Credibility is earned slowly — by hitting announced targets — so the gain arrives with a lag, and the speed of disinflation should match it: with inertia and partial credibility, a cold-turkey disinflation would have cost more unemployment than Chile's gradual path. The conclusion credits the region's success to the combination of fiscal discipline and "the restricted discretion embedded in IT".

## Key mechanisms / model

**Choosing an exchange rate regime (Section 2).** Benefits of giving up the currency (dollarization, union, a fully credible board): lower inflation, no currency risk premium, no transaction costs, no currency mismatch. Benefits of a float: real exchange rate flexibility, stabilization policy, seigniorage, lender of last resort. Which dominates depends on optimum-currency-area features (factor mobility, price and wage flexibility, openness, shock symmetry, diversification) and on financial ones (depth of hedging markets, ability to issue foreign debt in domestic currency). A history of high inflation that has left assets and liabilities in foreign currency limits the gain from floating, because exchange rate effects restrict monetary independence. The welfare schedules of Figure 2.1 summarise the cases; the consensus for countries integrated into capital markets had moved to the "corners hypothesis" (welfare highest at the two extremes).

**Why the alternative anchors fail.**
- *Exchange rate anchor:* easy to monitor and quickly credible, but credibility lasts only while the peg holds, and holding it is very costly when promises not to devalue are doubted — "when unemployment is high or the health of the banking system is in jeopardy". With an open capital account and weak financial regulation, fixing invites undue risk taking: the interest rate spread net of expected devaluation draws capital inflows, credit and spending boom, the real exchange rate appreciates, and a sudden reversal of flows sets up a crisis (Chile early 1980s, Mexico early 1990s, Asia 1997).
- *Money anchor:* works only with a stable money demand. After high and variable inflation, agents learn to economize on money, and when inflation falls hysteresis breaks the old demand relation (less money is held at the same inflation as before), so money targets become unreliable.

**What IT requires (Svensson, King):** a public medium-term target, institutional commitment to price stability, and a transparent strategy built on a conditional inflation forecast, with accountability. The target is the ultimate objective, the forecast the intermediate one, and the policy rate is raised when the forecast exceeds the target. Its weakness is that inflation is not directly controlled and acts with lags, so rigidly chasing the target after a temporary shock can cost output; the remedies are ranges, core-inflation targets, excluding indirect taxes, interest and energy from the index, and longer horizons. Emerging countries typically start disinflating before having a full framework, announce annual targets once progress is made, and phase in the other components.

**Chile's structural model (Section 6).** Quarterly equations for core inflation (a weighted average of tradable and non-tradable inflation plus expected inflation), wage inflation (lagged inflation for indexation plus expected inflation for forward-looking contracts), the output gap (its lag, the terms of trade, the lagged real rate, capital inflows), unemployment (Okun's law), the current account, the exchange rate inside the band, and headline inflation. Expected inflation, measured from nominal versus real interest rates on comparable instruments, depends on the forward-looking target, a four-quarter moving average of past inflation and a forecast-error term. For the disinflation counterfactuals a policy reaction function is added (extending Taylor and Clarida et al.): the real policy rate responds to the gap between expected and target inflation, to the current account deficit against a 4.5% of GDP target, and to its own lag.

What carries the results: (i) the target enters expectations, and expectations enter wages and prices — remove that and the target is just an announcement; (ii) wage indexation and backward-looking expectations give inertia, which is what makes fast disinflation costly; (iii) credibility is partial and grows with track record. Simulation 1 replaces 1990s expectations formation with the one estimated before IT (to 1990:4), isolating the target's effect; Simulations 2 and 3 change the speed of the target path; a final run imposes full credibility (expectations equal the target).

## Main results / findings

- **Regime shift.** Among 18 Latin American countries the share of pegs fell from 67% in 1979 to 23% in 2000 by the IMF classification (Figure 3.1); de facto classifications show the same decline. By 2000 Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Peru combined a free float with IT — the lower-right corner of Table 3.2.
- **Do the new floaters float?** An unconditional test of "fear of floating" (Calvo and Reinhart): the probability that the monthly change falls within a band. In Brazil the share of months with exchange rate moves within ±1% fell from 58.8 to 4.9 after the 1999 float (Table 3.1), and Mexico's also fell, but reserve volatility did not fall in either, which the authors attribute to Brazil using reserves to pay foreign debt and Mexico's put-option auctions. Chile's measures moved in the right direction but little, because its wide band was already de facto flexible. Canada and New Zealand, declared free floaters, show reserve volatility and little exchange rate volatility on the same test.
- **IT performance, 18 targeters 1986–1999.** All except Chile cut inflation between three years before and one year after adoption (Table 4.2), so disinflation tends to precede the regime. Convergence to stationary inflation took 8 quarters on average. Targets were generally met: an average absolute miss of 1.04 percentage points (Table 4.4); the Latin American record, except Colombia's, is comparable to other regions.
- **Disinflation costs.** Sacrifice ratios around adoption were very low, even negative, for three of five Latin American targeters and for recent targeters elsewhere, but positive for old industrial targeters (Table 4.5). In Chile and Peru they turned from positive before IT to negative after, whereas old targeters outside the region went from -0.32 to +0.19 on average (Table 4.6). The authors' reading: IT need not cut disinflation costs where inflation was already low, but there is "some evidence" that it does in emerging economies starting from moderate or high inflation — a gain from lower inflation and from credibility.
- **Output volatility** fell after adoption in 10 of 11 targeters, to an average of 2.4 against 3.3 for industrial non-targeters (Table 4.7).
- **Chile: something happened after the target.** Phillips-curve, reduced-form and ARIMA forecasts estimated on pre-IT data lie well above actual inflation in the 1990s (Figures 6.1–6.2), as do rolling-VAR forecasts (Figures 6.3–6.4). Consensus Forecasts expectations converge toward the announced targets over time (Table 6.1), read as targets gaining credibility through attainment.
- **Chile: the expectations channel.** With pre-IT expectations formation, simulated core inflation is above the benchmark, with a clear break from late 1996 (Table 6.3): the target's effect became important only some time after adoption, in the year the central bank announced a 6.5% target for 1996 after a 9% target and 8.2% actual inflation in 1995.
- **Chile: speed of disinflation.** Under partial credibility the cold-turkey path converges slowly toward its target and raises unemployment; the model's sacrifice ratio is –1.26 for cold turkey against –0.95 for the gradualist path (–1.26 and -0.99 with Consensus Forecasts expectations), which the authors read as cold turkey being costlier. With full credibility imposed, the cold-turkey ratio becomes –0.529, below the gradualist one, so the authors bound the true cold-turkey cost between –1.26 and –0.529. The ranking of gradualism versus shock therapy thus depends on credibility.

## Limitations and caveats

- The cross-country comparisons are descriptive: small samples, fixed windows around adoption, HP-filter trends, no controls for shocks or for selection (countries adopt IT after disinflation is under way). The fear-of-floating test is explicitly unconditional on fundamentals, and reserve volatility under floats is biased upward by portfolio swaps and valuation changes the authors cannot remove.
- For Chile the authors acknowledge rival explanations of the disinflation — earlier structural reforms, fiscal orthodoxy, the real appreciation with early-1990s capital inflows; the VAR exercise does not identify the target's contribution, and the structural model attributes it through the assumed expectations channel. They also note that with full credibility the expected-inflation coefficients in the price and wage equations could themselves be higher.
- The sign convention of the sacrifice ratios is not stated and is not consistent across sections: in Section 4 a negative ratio is read as a low (even favourable) cost, while in Section 6 a more negative ratio (–1.26 vs –0.95) is read as a larger cost. Read the comparisons as the authors' rankings, not as comparable magnitudes.
- Text and tables disagree in several places: Israel's average absolute miss is 1.67 in the text and 1.62 in Table 4.4; the average sacrifice ratio of old targeters outside the region is 0.88 in the text and 0.77 in Table 4.5; the non-targeters' average is 0.30 in the text and 0.39 in Table 4.6; inflation at adoption is 25% and 17% for Chile and Israel in the text and 29.0 and 18.5 in Table 4.3; the text puts Brazil's inflation at adoption below 3%, while Table 4.3 shows 8.3 (measured two quarters ahead). Table 4.5 is titled 1998-2000 although it covers adoptions back to 1989. In Table 6.4 the "Soft" and "Aggressive" column labels are the reverse of the text's description (the gradual path cuts the target by 0.5 point a year; the cold-turkey path sets 3% from 1996).
- Damaged passages: equations (6.1)–(6.9) and the estimated model in Table 6.2 have Greek letters reduced to plain characters and subscripts on separate lines; the reaction function (6.9) cannot be read. In Table 6.2 the coefficient on the lagged real rate in the output-gap equation prints as positive (0.427), which the text does not discuss; whether a sign was lost cannot be told from the file. Table 6.1's early rows have fewer entries than columns, so which value belongs to which column (Consensus, VAR1, VAR2, target) is ambiguous for 1991–1995. Figures survive as axis labels only. Footnote 17 gives the year of the Bank of England's independence as "199???". Two citations ("Banana et al. 1999", "Stealthier et al. 2000") match no author in the text and appear corrupted. The reference list is partial: it starts mid-entry and the page numbering jumps from 32 to 35. The cover page (Documento de Trabajo Nº 230, Noviembre 2002) names only Vittorio Corbo.
